name: Economics
notes: Competency areas and test-item counts from the official FBLA Economics guideline (2026-2027 edition, 'Updated August 2026', study guide pp. 5-6): https://greektrack-fbla-public.s3.amazonaws.com/files/1/High%20School%20Competitive%20Events%20Resources/Individual%20Guidelines/Objective%20Tests/Economics.pdf . Format: 50 minutes, 100 multiple-choice questions, online. Official items per area: Fundamental Economic Concepts 15, Nature of Business 15, Economic Systems 15, Government's Impact on Business 5, Cost/Profit Relationships 10, Economic Indicators 15, Global Trade 25. Objectives are aligned to MBA Research National Business Administration Standards (EC codes). This bank is still lighter on Global Trade and Economic Indicators, and heavier on Government's Impact on Business, than the official test. Questions are original practice items written for this site, not official FBLA items.

questions.q: Which best describes economic scarcity?
choices: A temporary shortage that appears when a price ceiling is set below equilibrium
The goods a government decides to ration during a war or other emergency
Unlimited wants exceeding the limited resources available to satisfy them
The total amount of goods and services a country produces in one year
questions.explain: Scarcity is the gap between unlimited wants and limited resources. A shortage from a price ceiling is a symptom of a market problem, not the definition of scarcity.

questions.q: What is the opportunity cost of a choice?
choices: The profit a firm earns after paying all of its fixed costs
The total money spent on a purchase, including sales tax
The price paid for a good minus its cost of production
The value of the next-best alternative given up when a choice is made
questions.explain: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative forgone. Money spent is an explicit cost, not an opportunity cost.

questions.q: Which factor of production is the initiative to start a business and the willingness to bear its risks?
choices: Labour
Capital
Land
Entrepreneurship
questions.explain: Entrepreneurship is the fourth factor of production: the entrepreneur organizes land, labour and capital and bears the risk of the venture. Labour is human effort paid with wages, not the risk-taking role.

questions.q: In the circular flow model, what do households provide to firms in the factor market?
choices: Finished goods and services
Consumer spending on products
Tax revenue and fees
Labour, land and capital
questions.explain: Households own the factors of production and supply them to firms for income. Goods and services flow the other way, through the product market.

questions.q: A point inside a production possibilities curve indicates that the economy is:
choices: operating at full employment with efficient allocation
unable to produce that combination of goods with current resources
operating inefficiently, with unemployed or underused resources
experiencing rapid economic growth
questions.explain: Points inside the curve are attainable but inefficient, because resources are idle or misallocated. Points on the curve are efficient.

questions.q: Which characteristic best defines a public good?
choices: Excludable but non-rival
Rival and excludable
Rival but non-excludable
Non-rival and non-excludable
questions.explain: A public good is non-rival (one person's use does not reduce another's) and non-excludable (no one can be barred from using it). Excludable but non-rival describes a club good.

questions.q: A country has a comparative advantage in producing a good when it can produce that good at:
choices: the lowest total cost in dollars
a higher output per worker than any other country in every good
the highest absolute productivity of any good
a lower opportunity cost than another country
questions.explain: Comparative advantage depends on opportunity cost, not on absolute cost or productivity. A country can lack an absolute advantage and still have a comparative one.

questions.q: Marginal cost is best defined as:
choices: total cost divided by the total number of units produced
the price of a unit minus its average variable cost
fixed costs spread evenly over all units produced
the change in total cost from producing one additional unit
questions.explain: Marginal cost is the change in total cost from one more unit. Dividing total cost by output gives average total cost.

questions.q: Which event would cause a rightward shift of the demand curve for a normal good?
choices: A decrease in consumer income
An increase in the price of the good itself
An increase in consumer income
A decrease in the price of the good itself
questions.explain: A change in the good's own price moves along the curve rather than shifting it. Rising income increases demand for normal goods.

questions.q: Which change would shift the supply curve for a product to the left?
choices: An increase in the price of the product itself
A technological improvement that lowers production costs
A subsidy paid to producers
An increase in the cost of raw materials
questions.explain: Higher input costs reduce the quantity firms are willing to supply at each price, shifting supply left. The other options shift supply right or move along the curve.

questions.q: When the market price is above equilibrium, what happens?
choices: A shortage occurs and the price tends to rise
Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
A surplus occurs and the price tends to fall
The market clears immediately
questions.explain: At a price above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a surplus that pushes the price down toward equilibrium.

questions.q: The price of a good rises 10% and the quantity demanded falls 20%. The absolute price elasticity of demand is closest to:
choices: 2.0, so demand is elastic
0.5, so demand is inelastic
10, so demand is perfectly elastic
0.2, so demand is unit elastic
questions.explain: Elasticity is 20% divided by 10%, which is 2.0. Since it is above 1, demand is elastic.

questions.q: Which good is most likely to have inelastic demand?
choices: Restaurant meals
A specific brand of cereal
Gasoline in the short run
Luxury cars
questions.explain: In the short run, drivers cannot quickly switch cars, commutes or transit, so gasoline has few substitutes and quantity demanded barely responds to price. Restaurant meals, one cereal brand and luxury cars all have close substitutes or can be put off.

questions.q: Diminishing marginal returns occur when:
choices: total output begins to decline with any additional input
average costs fall steadily as the firm's output increases
fixed costs rise with each additional unit the firm produces
each added unit of a variable input adds less output than the one before
questions.explain: Diminishing marginal returns mean the extra output from each added unit of a variable input falls, even while total output may still rise.

questions.q: Consumer surplus is the difference between:
choices: the market price and the cost of production
total revenue and total cost
the market price and the seller's minimum acceptable price
the maximum a buyer is willing to pay and the price actually paid
questions.explain: Consumer surplus is the gain to buyers: their willingness to pay minus the market price. The option about a seller's minimum acceptable price describes producer surplus.

questions.q: Which type of trade agreement removes tariffs among its members but lets each member keep its own tariffs on goods from non-member countries?
choices: A free trade area
A customs union
A common market
An economic and monetary union
questions.explain: In a free trade area, members drop tariffs on each other's goods but each sets its own tariffs on outsiders. A customs union adds a common external tariff, a common market also frees the movement of labour and capital, and a monetary union adds a shared currency.

questions.q: The Latin phrase ceteris paribus means:
choices: all prices in the economy change together
the economy is operating at full employment
all other relevant factors are held constant
consumers always act in their own best interest
questions.explain: Economists use ceteris paribus to isolate the effect of one variable by holding others constant.

questions.q: Which statement is normative?
choices: Raising the minimum wage increases teen unemployment
The minimum wage is a type of price floor
Each $1 increase in the minimum wage reduces hours worked by 2%
The government should raise the minimum wage to $15 per hour
questions.explain: 'Should' statements express value judgments and are normative. The others are positive, testable claims.

questions.q: Which is a microeconomic topic?
choices: The national inflation rate
The federal budget deficit
Monetary policy set by the central bank
A single firm's pricing decision
questions.explain: Microeconomics studies individual households, firms and markets. The other three concern the economy as a whole.

questions.q: A savings account pays 3% interest a year while inflation runs at 5% a year. The saver's real rate of return is closest to:
questions.explain: Real return is roughly the nominal rate minus inflation: 3% - 5% = -2%. The balance grows, but it buys less each year, which is how inflation hurts savers and lenders.

questions.q: Marginal utility is:
choices: the total satisfaction from all units consumed
the average satisfaction per unit consumed
the additional satisfaction from consuming one more unit
the price a consumer pays per unit
questions.explain: Marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from one more unit. Consumers maximize utility where marginal utility per dollar is equal across goods.

questions.q: Which function does the price system perform?
choices: Guarantees every buyer a fair share of scarce goods
Allocates scarce goods to those willing and able to pay
Eliminates all opportunity costs
Prevents shortages in every market
questions.explain: Prices ration scarce goods to those willing and able to pay. Prices do not guarantee fairness and do not eliminate opportunity costs.

questions.q: If the price of tea rises and, as a result, demand for coffee increases, tea and coffee are:
choices: complements
inferior goods
normal goods
substitutes
questions.explain: Substitutes can replace each other. A higher tea price pushes buyers toward coffee, so demand for coffee rises (the whole curve shifts right).

questions.q: Hot dogs and hot dog buns are complements. If the price of hot dogs rises, what happens in the market for buns?
choices: Demand for buns shifts left, so their price and quantity both fall
Demand for buns shifts right, so their price and quantity both rise
Supply of buns shifts left, so their price rises and quantity falls
Quantity of buns demanded rises along an unchanged demand curve
questions.explain: A higher hot dog price means fewer hot dogs are bought, so fewer buns are wanted at every price. Demand for buns shifts left, lowering their equilibrium price and quantity; bun supply has not changed.

questions.q: If both demand and supply increase, the equilibrium price:
choices: rises, because demand growth always outweighs supply growth
falls, because more supply always pushes the price down
could rise, fall or stay the same, depending on which shift is larger
stays exactly the same, because the two shifts cancel out
questions.explain: Both shifts raise equilibrium quantity for certain, but their opposing effects on price depend on which shift is larger.

questions.q: Which form of business has a single owner who bears unlimited personal liability for business debts?
choices: Sole proprietorship
C corporation
Limited liability company
Nonprofit corporation
questions.explain: A sole proprietor and the business are legally the same, so personal assets can be reached for business debts.

questions.q: A key disadvantage of a C corporation for U.S. federal tax purposes is:
choices: unlimited personal liability for all of its shareholders
owners must pay self-employment tax on all profit
shareholders are not allowed to sell or transfer their shares
double taxation of corporate profits and of dividends paid to shareholders
questions.explain: A C corporation pays corporate income tax on its profit, and shareholders pay personal tax again on dividends. LLCs (by default) and S corporations (by election) are pass-through entities that avoid this.

questions.q: Which statement about liability in a limited partnership is correct?
choices: Every partner has unlimited personal liability for the firm's debts
Every partner's liability is limited to the amount invested
Limited partners have unlimited liability; general partners are protected
General partners have unlimited liability; limited partners risk only their investment
questions.explain: A limited partnership needs at least one general partner, who manages the firm and has unlimited liability. Limited partners usually stay out of management and can lose only what they invested.

questions.q: Which section of a business plan describes the target market and the competition in detail?
choices: Market analysis
Executive summary
Operations plan
Financial projections
questions.explain: The market analysis covers target customers, industry size and competitors in detail. The executive summary only previews the whole plan, and the operations and financial sections cover how the business runs and its numbers.

questions.q: Which group is an internal stakeholder of a business?
choices: Suppliers
Customers
Employees
Competitors
questions.explain: Internal stakeholders work within or own the firm. Employees are internal; suppliers, customers and competitors are external.

questions.q: The four functions of management are:
choices: buying, selling, producing and distributing
hiring, firing, paying and training
budgeting, auditing, taxing and reporting
planning, organizing, leading and controlling
questions.explain: The classic management functions are planning, organizing, leading (directing) and controlling.

questions.q: The four Ps of the marketing mix are:
choices: price, place, purchase and profit
product, process, people and profit
planning, pricing, packaging and public relations
product, price, place and promotion
questions.explain: The marketing mix is product, price, place and promotion. Some texts add people, process and physical evidence for services.

questions.q: The break-even point occurs when:
choices: total revenue equals total cost
profit is maximized
marginal cost equals marginal revenue
fixed costs equal variable costs
questions.explain: At break-even, total revenue equals total cost and profit is zero. Marginal cost equal to marginal revenue is the profit-maximizing rule.

questions.q: A U.S. clothing company moves its sewing work from Ohio to a factory it owns in Vietnam, while its design team stays in New York. This practice is called:
choices: Insourcing
Licensing
Offshoring
Exporting
questions.explain: Offshoring moves business activities to another country, here to the company's own factory. Outsourcing would mean hiring an outside firm, licensing lets another firm use your brand or patent for a fee, and exporting is selling goods abroad.

questions.q: A nonprofit corporation differs from a for-profit corporation mainly because:
choices: it is not allowed to hire paid employees
it is not allowed to charge for goods or services
it is exempt from every tax, including payroll taxes
its earnings cannot be distributed to owners as profit
questions.explain: Nonprofits may charge fees, earn revenue and hire staff, and most still owe payroll taxes. The key difference is that any surplus cannot be distributed to owners, members or directors as profit.

questions.q: Which business structure protects all of its owners' personal assets from business debts and, with two or more owners, is taxed as a partnership by default for U.S. federal tax purposes?
choices: A C corporation (C corp)
A general partnership (GP)
A limited liability company (LLC)
An S corporation (S corp)
questions.explain: A multi-member LLC shields every owner's personal assets and is taxed as a partnership (pass-through) unless it elects otherwise. A general partnership has the same tax default but unlimited liability, and an S corporation gets pass-through treatment only by election, under its own rules.

questions.q: The main advantage of buying a franchise over starting an independent business is:
choices: complete control over product design
no royalty or fee obligations
an established brand and operating system
exemption from the franchisor's standards
questions.explain: Franchisees trade some independence and ongoing fees for a proven brand, training and systems. Franchisees usually do pay royalties and must follow standards.

questions.q: In a SWOT analysis, which element is an external factor the business cannot directly control?
choices: Strength
Core competency
Weakness
Threat
questions.explain: Threats (and opportunities) are external. Strengths and weaknesses are internal and under the firm's influence.

questions.q: Which form of intellectual property protects a brand name and logo used to identify goods?
choices: Patent
Copyright
Trade secret
Trademark
questions.explain: Trademarks protect names, logos and slogans that identify the source of goods. Patents cover inventions, and copyrights cover creative works.

questions.q: A U.S. utility patent protects a novel invention or process for how long from the filing date?
choices: 10 years
Life of the inventor plus 70 years
50 years
20 years
questions.explain: A utility patent lasts 20 years from the filing date. Copyright for works by an individual lasts life plus 70 years, which is a common mix-up.

questions.q: Which body of U.S. law governs most contracts for the sale of goods, such as a retailer buying inventory from a manufacturer?
choices: Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code
Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act
The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938
The federal Securities Act of 1933
questions.explain: UCC Article 2, adopted by every state except Louisiana, governs sales of goods, whether between merchants or with consumers. The other laws cover antitrust, wages and securities.

questions.q: Besides offer, acceptance and consideration, a legally enforceable contract generally requires:
choices: a notary's signature and official seal
a signed written document in every case
capacity of the parties and a legal purpose
at least two witnesses to the signing
questions.explain: Enforceable contracts need capacity (parties able to contract) and lawful purpose. Writing is required only for certain contracts under the Statute of Frauds.

questions.q: Which is an example of a variable cost for a bakery?
choices: The annual insurance premium on the shop
Monthly rent on the building
Flour and sugar used in each batch of product
The salary of the owner-manager
questions.explain: Variable costs rise with output. Ingredients rise with each batch, while rent, insurance and salaries are generally fixed in the short run.

questions.q: Which best describes a business's mission statement?
choices: Its long-term purpose and reason for existing
Its sales target for the coming year
A list of its current products and prices
The daily schedule its employees follow
questions.explain: A mission statement states why the business exists. Sales targets are goals, which are narrower and time-bound.

questions.q: Which best describes market segmentation?
choices: Selling the same product to every consumer in the same way
Eliminating competitors through a merger
Setting a single price for all customers
Dividing a market into groups of buyers with shared characteristics
questions.explain: Segmentation groups buyers by traits such as age, income or needs so each group can be targeted with a tailored marketing mix.

questions.q: In a pure market economy, who primarily decides what goods are produced?
choices: Government planners, through production quotas
Labour unions, through collective bargaining
Consumers and producers, through prices
The central bank, through interest rates
questions.explain: In a market economy, prices signal what consumers want, and producers respond to those signals to earn profit.

questions.q: Which best describes a command economy?
choices: A central government makes most production and allocation decisions
Prices are set by supply and demand, with no government role
All private property is abolished, including personal belongings
All trade with other countries is prohibited by law
questions.explain: In a command economy, a central authority plans what, how and for whom goods are produced. The other options describe a market economy or extreme cases.

questions.q: The United States is best described as which type of economy?
choices: Command economy
Traditional economy
Mixed market economy
Subsistence economy
questions.explain: The U.S. relies mainly on markets but has significant government regulation, taxation and public goods, which makes it a mixed economy.

questions.q: A traditional economy relies primarily on:
choices: customs and beliefs passed down through generations
central planning by a national government agency
auction markets where prices change every day
international aid from wealthier countries
questions.explain: Traditional economies answer the basic economic questions through customs passed down over generations.

questions.q: Which is a core feature of capitalism?
choices: Government ownership of major industries
Fixed prices set by law for all goods
Equal distribution of income to all households
Private ownership of businesses and productive resources
questions.explain: Capitalism is built on private ownership of the factors of production and market-determined prices.

questions.q: Which is most characteristic of socialist economic systems?
choices: Widespread private ownership of land
Unrestricted foreign trade
Public ownership of major means of production
Prices set by individual firms only
questions.explain: Socialism generally places key productive assets in public or collective ownership, although models vary widely.

questions.q: When a society decides how its output is shared among people, through wages, prices or rationing, which basic economic question is it answering?
choices: What to produce
How to produce
For whom to produce
When to produce
questions.explain: Deciding who gets the output is the 'for whom' question. 'What' is about which goods to make, and 'how' is about which resources and methods to use.

questions.q: The 'invisible hand' concept, associated with Adam Smith, refers to:
choices: government price controls that steer markets toward fair prices
foreign aid programs that move resources to poorer nations
a central bank quietly managing the money supply
self-interest in markets unintentionally promoting society's welfare
questions.explain: Smith argued that individuals pursuing their own gain through voluntary exchange can produce socially beneficial outcomes.

questions.q: Why are secure property rights important in a market economy?
choices: They eliminate the need for prices in most markets
They guarantee every household an equal income
They give owners incentives to invest, save and trade
They prevent all forms of competition between firms
questions.explain: Secure property rights let owners keep the returns from their investment and trade, which encourages productive activity.

questions.q: A major problem with central planning is:
choices: too much consumer choice, which wastes resources on variety
excessive competition between firms, which drives prices too low
too much accurate price information for planners to process
shortages and surpluses, because no market prices signal scarcity
questions.explain: Without prices that reflect scarcity, planners struggle to allocate resources efficiently, which leads to shortages and surpluses.

questions.q: In economics, equity refers to:
choices: the fairness of how income and goods are distributed
producing goods at the lowest possible total cost
the speed at which the economy grows over time
the amount of money circulating in the economy
questions.explain: Equity is about fairness in distribution. Efficiency is about getting the most output from scarce resources. The two often trade off.

questions.q: An allocation of resources is Pareto efficient when:
choices: every person in the economy receives an identical income
total output is maximized no matter what resources it uses
no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off
the government sets every price equal to the cost of production
questions.explain: Pareto efficiency means no reallocation can improve one person's position without harming another. It says nothing about equal incomes.

questions.q: Which describes a market failure?
choices: Markets allocating resources inefficiently, such as through unpriced pollution
Many small firms competing to sell an identical product at the market price
Prices that fully reflect every cost and benefit of producing a good
An economy at full employment with stable prices and steady growth
questions.explain: Market failure occurs when markets misallocate resources, often because of externalities, public goods or market power.

questions.q: Pollution from a factory that harms nearby residents, who are not compensated, is an example of:
choices: a positive externality
a merit good
a public good
a negative externality
questions.explain: A negative externality imposes an uncompensated cost on third parties. Its market price does not reflect that cost, so too much is produced.

questions.q: Which is the best example of a public good?
choices: National defence
Fish in the open ocean
A streaming service subscription
A restaurant meal
questions.explain: National defence is non-rival and non-excludable. Ocean fish are non-excludable but rival (a common resource), a streaming subscription is excludable (a club good), and a restaurant meal is a private good.

questions.q: Which is an example of a merit good?
choices: Cigarettes
Public education
Luxury yachts
Designer clothing
questions.explain: Merit goods are considered socially desirable and are often subsidized or provided publicly, such as education and vaccines.

questions.q: Privatization refers to:
choices: transferring government-owned enterprises to private ownership
the government buying private companies and running them
an increase in government spending on public services
the creation of a new government-owned corporation
questions.explain: Privatization moves assets or services from public to private ownership, such as through a sale of a state-owned company.

questions.q: Which trade-off is central to every economic system?
choices: Price stability versus scarcity
Efficiency versus equity
Inflation versus consumer spending
Tax revenue versus deficits
questions.explain: Every system must balance getting the most from scarce resources (efficiency) against how fairly they are shared (equity).

questions.q: Division of labour increases productivity mainly because:
choices: workers can avoid every task they find unpleasant or boring
workers build skill in a task and lose less time switching between tasks
machines are no longer needed once tasks are split up
the prices of the goods produced always fall right away
questions.explain: Specialization builds skill and efficiency. Adam Smith's pin factory example illustrates the point.

questions.q: Specialization and trade benefit nations because they allow each nation to:
choices: eliminate scarcity entirely for all of its citizens
consume beyond what its own production possibilities would allow
remove the need for money in international exchange
guarantee the same living standard as its trading partners
questions.explain: Trade lets countries consume combinations of goods outside their own production possibilities curve, which raises total welfare.

questions.q: Fiscal policy refers to:
choices: setting interest rates and reserve requirements
government decisions about taxation and spending
managing the exchange rate
control of the money supply by the Federal Reserve
questions.explain: Fiscal policy uses taxes and government spending. Interest rates and reserve requirements are monetary policy tools.

questions.q: In the U.S., monetary policy is conducted primarily by:
choices: Congress
the Federal Reserve System
the Treasury Department's tax office
the Securities and Exchange Commission
questions.explain: The Federal Reserve sets a target range for the federal funds rate and influences the money supply. Congress, with the President, makes fiscal decisions about taxes and spending.

questions.q: A per-unit tax levied on sellers shifts the supply curve:
choices: to the right
to the left
not at all
to become perfectly elastic
questions.explain: A tax raises sellers' costs, so they supply less at each price. This shifts supply to the left, raising the price buyers pay.

questions.q: A government subsidy paid to producers generally results in:
choices: a decrease in supply
a rightward shift of the supply curve
an increase in the price consumers pay
a shortage in the market
questions.explain: A subsidy lowers producers' effective costs, so they supply more at each price, shifting supply right and typically lowering the price consumers pay.

questions.q: A tariff is best defined as:
choices: a tax on imported goods
a limit on the physical quantity of exports
a government payment to exporters
a fee charged by banks for currency exchange
questions.explain: A tariff is a tax on imports. It raises domestic prices and generates government revenue.

questions.q: An import quota differs from a tariff because a quota:
choices: collects revenue for the government
limits the physical quantity of imports allowed
always raises prices less than a tariff
applies only to services
questions.explain: A quota caps the quantity of imports, while a tariff taxes them. A quota generally does not produce government tariff revenue.

questions.q: The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 primarily aims to:
choices: regulate the interest rates banks may charge
outlaw monopolization and agreements that restrain trade
set a national minimum wage for workers
protect copyrights on books, music and films
questions.explain: The Sherman Act bans contracts and conspiracies in restraint of trade and the monopolization (or attempted monopolization) of markets. Simply being the only seller because of a better product is not itself illegal.

questions.q: Which U.S. federal agency requires public companies to disclose financial information and takes action against insider trading?
choices: Federal Trade Commission
Securities and Exchange Commission
Federal Reserve
Department of Labor
questions.explain: The SEC enforces federal securities laws, including disclosure rules for public companies and the ban on insider trading. The FTC handles consumer protection and competition, and the Fed runs monetary policy.

questions.q: A binding minimum wage set above the equilibrium wage typically causes:
choices: a surplus of labour, meaning unemployment
a shortage of workers for every employer
lower wages for all workers
an increase in labour demand
questions.explain: A binding wage floor raises the quantity of labour supplied above the quantity demanded, creating unemployment among those seeking work.

questions.q: Rent control set below the equilibrium rent most likely causes:
choices: a shortage of rental housing
a surplus of rental housing
higher rents for all tenants
more new apartment construction
questions.explain: A binding price ceiling lowers quantity supplied and raises quantity demanded, leaving a housing shortage.

questions.q: Deadweight loss from a per-unit tax is largest when:
choices: supply and demand are both perfectly inelastic
demand and supply are relatively elastic
the tax rate is zero
the market is a monopoly with no competition
questions.explain: Deadweight loss grows with the responsiveness of quantity to price. Elastic supply and demand let the tax shrink trade more.

questions.q: If demand is perfectly inelastic, the burden of a per-unit tax falls:
choices: entirely on consumers
entirely on producers
equally on consumers and producers
on the government only
questions.explain: When buyers cannot reduce quantity demanded, sellers can pass the full tax on through higher prices. Tax incidence follows relative elasticity.

questions.q: In a simple model with no taxes or imports, the marginal propensity to consume is 0.8. The government spending multiplier is:
questions.explain: The multiplier is 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / 0.2 = 5.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the federal budget deficit from the national debt?
choices: The deficit is the cumulative total owed; the debt is the one-year shortfall
The debt is the cumulative total owed; the deficit is the one-year excess of spending over revenue
They are identical measures
The deficit is always larger than the debt
questions.explain: The deficit is an annual flow (spending exceeds revenue in one year). The debt is the accumulated stock of past deficits net of surpluses.

questions.q: Which U.S. federal law prohibits 'unfair or deceptive acts or practices' in commerce and is the main basis for federal action against false advertising?
choices: Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act
Section 7 of the Clayton Act
The Glass-Steagall Banking Act of 1933
The Fair Credit Reporting Act of 1970
questions.explain: Section 5 of the FTC Act (amended by the Wheeler-Lea Act of 1938) bans unfair or deceptive acts or practices, and the FTC uses it against false advertising. Clayton Act Section 7 covers mergers, Glass-Steagall separated commercial and investment banking, and the FCRA covers credit reports.

questions.q: A firm faces elastic demand (elasticity of 2.0). To increase total revenue, it should:
choices: raise its price
lower its price
keep its price constant and raise fixed costs
raise its variable costs
questions.explain: With elastic demand, the quantity gain from a price cut outweighs the lower price, so total revenue rises. Costs do not affect revenue.

questions.q: Economic profit equals:
choices: total revenue minus accounting (explicit) costs only
total revenue minus explicit and implicit costs
the net income reported on the income statement
total revenue minus variable costs only
questions.explain: Economic profit subtracts implicit costs such as forgone wages. Accounting profit ignores them, so it is usually higher.

questions.q: A firm sells 500 units at $12 each. Variable cost is $7 per unit and total fixed cost is $1,000. Its profit is:
questions.explain: Revenue is $6,000. Variable cost is $3,500 and fixed cost is $1,000, leaving $1,500. Ignoring fixed cost gives $2,500, a common trap.

questions.q: Fixed costs are $60,000, price is $50 per unit and variable cost is $30 per unit. The break-even quantity is:
choices: 1,200 units
3,000 units
2,000 units
6,000 units
questions.explain: Contribution margin is $20 per unit. Break-even quantity is $60,000 / $20 = 3,000 units.

questions.q: Total cost is $4,800 for 120 units of output. Average total cost is:
questions.explain: Average total cost is total cost divided by quantity: $4,800 / 120 = $40.

questions.q: Total cost rises from $500 to $560 when output increases from 10 to 12 units. The marginal cost of each added unit is:
questions.explain: Change in total cost is $60 and change in quantity is 2 units, so marginal cost is $30.

questions.q: In the short run, a firm should keep operating if the market price is at least:
choices: its average variable cost
its average total cost
its marginal cost of zero
its fixed cost per unit
questions.explain: Covering variable costs lets the firm pay part of its fixed costs. Below average variable cost, it should shut down in the short run.

questions.q: In a perfectly competitive market in long-run equilibrium, firms earn:
choices: large economic profits
zero economic profit
persistent losses
unlimited profit
questions.explain: Entry and exit drive economic profit to zero in the long run. Accounting profit may still be positive.

questions.q: Which cost is an implicit cost?
choices: Wages the business pays its part-time employees
Rent the business pays each month for its store
The salary the owner gives up by not working elsewhere
Electricity and water bills paid by the business
questions.explain: Implicit costs are the value of resources the owner supplies that are not paid in cash, such as forgone wages. The other three are explicit payments.

questions.q: Long-run average cost falls as output increases because of:
choices: diminishing returns
economies of scale
rising fixed costs
excise taxes
questions.explain: Economies of scale lower average cost as output grows, such as through bulk purchasing and specialization. Diminishing returns is a short-run concept.

questions.q: Gross domestic product measures:
choices: the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period
the total income earned by a country's citizens and firms, wherever they produce
the value of all goods sold in a country in a year, including intermediate goods
the total amount the federal government spends on goods and services in a year
questions.explain: GDP counts final goods and services produced domestically in a period. It excludes intermediate goods to avoid double counting.

questions.q: The Consumer Price Index measures:
choices: the average change in the selling prices that domestic producers receive
the total value of all final goods and services a country produces
the average change over time in prices urban consumers pay for a basket of goods and services
the interest rate banks charge their most creditworthy customers
questions.explain: CPI tracks the cost of a fixed basket of consumer goods and services over time and is the most common inflation gauge. Producer selling prices are the PPI, and total final output is GDP.

questions.q: A person who is actively looking for work but currently has no job is counted as:
choices: employed
not in the labour force
unemployed
underemployed only
questions.explain: The BLS counts people who have no job, have searched for work recently, and are available for work as unemployed.

questions.q: Real GDP differs from nominal GDP because real GDP:
choices: ignores government spending
adjusts for changes in the price level
includes only exports
counts only household consumption
questions.explain: Real GDP removes the effect of price changes, so it reflects actual changes in output. Nominal GDP uses current prices.

questions.q: A common definition of a recession in the business cycle is:
choices: two consecutive quarters of declining real GDP
a rise in the inflation rate (CPI) above 5% a year
a fall in the unemployment rate for two quarters
a long period of rising stock market prices
questions.explain: The two-consecutive-quarters rule is a common rule of thumb. The official U.S. call is made by the NBER and considers several indicators.

questions.q: If the U.S. dollar appreciates against the euro, U.S. exports to Europe become:
choices: cheaper for Europeans
more expensive for Europeans
unchanged in price to Europeans
exempt from tariffs
questions.explain: A stronger dollar means each dollar buys fewer euros, so U.S. goods cost European buyers more in euros.

questions.q: In one hour, Country A can make 10 shirts or 5 phones, and Country B can make 6 shirts or 2 phones. Which statement is correct?
choices: Country A should make shirts, because it makes more shirts per hour than B
Country B has a comparative advantage in shirts, and Country A in phones
Country A has a comparative advantage in both goods, so trade cannot help
Country B has a comparative advantage in phones, since it makes fewer of them
questions.explain: Country A gives up 0.5 phone per shirt; Country B gives up only 1/3 phone, so B has the comparative advantage in shirts. A gives up 2 shirts per phone versus B's 3, so A has it in phones. A has the absolute advantage in both goods, but no country can have the comparative advantage in both.

questions.q: The current account of the U.S. balance of payments includes:
choices: trade in goods and services, plus net income and transfers
only foreign direct investment flowing into the country
only changes in the central bank's foreign currency reserves
only sales of government bonds to foreign investors
questions.explain: The current account covers trade in goods and services, net primary income and net transfers. Capital and financial accounts track investment flows.

questions.q: A trade deficit means:
choices: exports exceed imports
imports exceed exports
government spending exceeds tax revenue
the currency is fixed to another currency
questions.explain: A trade deficit means the country buys more from abroad than it sells. Government spending exceeding tax revenue is a budget deficit.

questions.q: The USMCA is a trade agreement among the United States, Canada and which other country?
choices: Brazil
Mexico
Japan
the European Union
questions.explain: USMCA (CUSMA in Canada) replaced NAFTA on July 1, 2020. At its first joint review on July 1, 2026 the U.S. declined to extend it, which starts annual reviews, but the agreement stays in force through 2036.

vocab.def: The condition in which unlimited wants exceed the limited resources available to satisfy them.
The value of the next-best alternative given up when a choice is made.
The inputs used to produce goods and services: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.
The factor of production that organizes land, labour and capital and bears the risk of a new venture.
A model showing how money, goods, services and factors of production flow between households and firms.
A graph showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources and technology.
A good that is non-rival and non-excludable, so private markets tend to underprovide it.
The ability of a producer to make a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.
Decision-making based on comparing the additional benefit of an action with its additional cost.
The additional satisfaction a consumer gains from consuming one more unit of a good.
As the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, all else equal.
As the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises, all else equal.
The price and quantity at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so there is no pressure to change.
The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.
Goods that are used together, so a fall in the price of one raises demand for the other.
A business owned and run by one person, who bears unlimited personal liability for its debts.
A business owned by two or more people who share profits, losses and management responsibilities.
A legal entity separate from its owners, which can own property, sue and be sued, and whose owners have limited liability.
A business form that shields owners from personal liability for business debts while allowing flexible tax treatment.
A written document describing a business's goals, market, operations, management and financial projections.
A planning tool that evaluates a business's internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats.
Any person or group affected by a business's decisions, such as owners, employees, customers, suppliers or the community.
The four Ps (product, price, place and promotion) a business combines to meet customer needs.
Dividing a broad market into groups of buyers who share characteristics or needs.
An arrangement in which a franchisee pays a fee and royalties to use a franchisor's brand, system and support.
A government grant giving an inventor exclusive rights to a new invention or process for a set period, 20 years from filing for utility patents in the U.S.
A word, name, symbol or design that identifies the source of goods or services and is protected from unauthorized use.
An economic system in which prices set by supply and demand guide most decisions about production and distribution.
An economic system in which a central authority makes most decisions about what, how and for whom goods are produced.
An economic system combining market allocation with significant government participation in the economy.
An economic system in which customs, habits and beliefs passed down over generations determine how goods are produced and shared.
An economic system based on private ownership of capital and the use of markets to allocate resources.
An economic system in which major means of production are owned publicly or collectively rather than privately.
Adam Smith's idea that self-interested market participants can unintentionally advance the wider social good.
A situation in which markets fail to allocate resources efficiently, such as because of externalities or public goods.
A cost or benefit of an economic activity that falls on third parties and is not reflected in market prices.
A good that society considers more beneficial than consumers may recognize, such as education, and that is often subsidized.
The transfer of government-owned assets or services to private ownership or management.
Splitting production into specialized tasks so each worker builds skill and output rises.
Government decisions about taxation and spending used to influence the level of economic activity.
Actions by a central bank, such as changing interest rates or the money supply, to influence the economy.
A tax on imported goods that raises their price and generates government revenue.
A government limit on the physical quantity of a good that may be imported or produced.
A government payment to a producer or consumer that lowers the effective cost of a good or activity.
A legal maximum price; when set below equilibrium, it causes a shortage.
A legal minimum price; when set above equilibrium, it causes a surplus.
An 1890 U.S. law that prohibits contracts and conspiracies in restraint of trade and the monopolization of markets.
A cost that does not change with the level of output in the short run, such as rent.
A cost that rises or falls with the level of output, such as raw materials.
The opportunity cost of resources a business owner supplies without a cash payment, such as forgone wages.
The output level at which total revenue equals total cost, so profit is zero.
Total revenue minus all costs, including implicit opportunity costs.
Falling long-run average cost as a firm increases its scale of output.
The market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period.
A measure of the average change over time in prices paid by urban consumers for a fixed basket of goods and services.
The percentage of the labour force that is actively seeking work but does not have a job.
The price of one currency in terms of another currency.
An increase in a currency's value relative to another currency, so it buys more of that currency.
The part of the balance of payments that records trade in goods and services, net income and net transfers.
A situation in which a country's imports of goods and services exceed its exports over a period.
